name: Common Turkic
region: From Mongolia across the Eurasian steppe, then to Anatolia, Central Asia, the Volga and northeastern Siberia
defining_innovation: Every Turkic language except Oghur, with z and š where Oghur has r and l. Its oldest form, Old Turkic, is known from the 8th-century Orkhon inscriptions.

chapters.title: Old Turkic
chapters.body:
Common Turkic enters history with the Türk (Göktürk) khaganate, founded in 552 on the Mongolian steppe, which within a generation reached from Manchuria to the Black Sea. Its successor, the Second Türk khaganate, raised the first Turkic texts: large stone monuments beside the Orkhon river in Mongolia. They were written in a runic-looking alphabet for Tonyukuk, the statesman who composed his own memorial (c. 720), and for the khagans Kül Tegin (732) and Bilge (735).

The inscriptions speak directly to their readers ('Hear my words well, Turkic lords and people!') and tell the history of the empire in a language that modern Turkic speakers can partly follow. Europeans could not read them until 1893, when the Danish linguist **Vilhelm Thomsen** deciphered the script.

chapters.title: Uyghur and Islam
chapters.body:
The Uyghur khaganate (744–840) that followed adopted a script derived from Sogdian, and after moving to the Tarim Basin the Uyghurs produced a large Buddhist and Manichaean literature in it. The Uyghur script later passed to the Mongols and from them to the Manchus.

From the 10th century, Turkic dynasties in Central Asia converted to Islam, and Arabic script, Arabic religious vocabulary and above all Persian cultural vocabulary spread through the Turkic languages. Over the next centuries migrations and conquests (Seljuk, Mongol, Timurid, Ottoman) carried Common Turkic west to the Balkans and north to the Arctic, and the branches recorded here took shape.

speakers.note: Every Turkic speaker except the Chuvash; the figure is uncertain mainly because counts of Azerbaijani speakers in Iran vary widely.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig (eds.). 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.
Johanson, Lars. 2021. Turkic. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

turning_points.title: The Türk khaganate
turning_points.description: The Türk khaganate unites the steppe from Mongolia to the Black Sea and spreads Common Turkic across it. The later branches grow out of the dialects of its successor states and confederations.

sources.citation: Golden, Peter B. 1992. An Introduction to the History of the Turkic Peoples. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz.

turning_points.title: The Orkhon inscriptions
turning_points.description: Monuments to Tonyukuk, Kül Tegin and Bilge Khagan are carved in the Old Turkic runic script, the first long Turkic texts. The script's origin, whether it was developed from Sogdian or another Aramaic-derived alphabet or partly from local signs, is debated.

sources.citation: Tekin, Talât. 1968. A Grammar of Orkhon Turkic. Bloomington: Indiana University.
Thomsen, Vilhelm. 1893. Déchiffrement des inscriptions de l'Orkhon et de l'Iénisséi. Copenhagen: Bianco Luno.

turning_points.title: Old Uyghur script
turning_points.description: The Uyghurs adopt a script derived from Sogdian and use it for a large Buddhist and Manichaean literature. It is later passed on to the Mongols and the Manchus.

sources.citation: Johanson, Lars & Éva Á. Csató, eds. 2022. The Turkic Languages, 2nd ed. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Islam, Arabic and Persian
turning_points.description: Conversion to Islam brings Arabic script and religious vocabulary into the Turkic languages, along with a deep layer of Persian cultural vocabulary that shapes Turkic literary languages for a thousand years.

sources.citation: Johanson, Lars. 2021. Turkic. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
